# Sprites are generated by a pipeline from a gitignored pack

The characters come from Ozzbit Games' free "male hero" pack, whose license reads: "Personal, non-commercial projects only. Modifications allowed. Resell not allowed. Credits required: Ozzbit Games". The original pack lives in `assets-src/`, which is gitignored, so the repository never redistributes it as a pack. `bun run sprites` runs recipes written in code over it: slices the 128×128 sheet into frames, makes eight hair-colour variants of one character, erases the sword from the shove animation by colour, and draws the emote balloons and the rooftop props from pixel grids written as text. Only the sheets the pipeline produces are committed. The pipeline runs on the owner's machine; CI and the Docker build use the committed sheets and never need the pack.

## Consequences

The game credits "Personagem: Ozzbit Games" (now "Herói: Ozzbit Games", see the amendment) in the README and in-game, carries no ads and stays non-commercial. A new character or prop is a recipe change plus a run of `bun run sprites` on a machine that has the pack; the README says how to ask for one. Anything drawn from a text grid (balloons, props) has no license strings attached and could be regenerated anywhere, but goes through the same command so there is one way to make art.

## Amendment: a second model, the skeleton knight

A second character model, a skeleton knight, is the owner's own art: no license restriction and no credit needed. It follows the same path as the hero: the source sheets (and the `.ase`) live in gitignored `assets-src/skeleton/`, and `bun run sprites` turns them into committed sheets with a recipe (`tools/sprites/src/skeleton.ts`). The eight characters stay eight and the protocol is unchanged: 0–3 are the hero with four hair colours, 4–7 the skeleton with four cape colours (the cape ramp is the only part recoloured; the red eyes stay). Each character gets its own sheet (`char-N.png`), each model its own atlas (`hero.json`, `skeleton.json`, with `credit` null for the skeleton), and `characters.json` ties them together for the client.

The skeleton art has idle, walk and sword swings but no run, jump or fall, so the recipe draws them from the existing frames: the walk leaned forward with the cape trailing for the run, the idle squashed into a crouch and an overhead-swing frame stretched with the cape pulled down and a leg tucked for the jump, and that body with the cape cut from the forward swing rotated to fly upward for the fall. The shove is the forward swing with its white slash trail erased (white blobs too large to be bone) and the sword kept. These drawn frames are a stand-in: a hand-drawn sheet from the owner in `assets-src/skeleton/` should replace them.

Since the hero is no longer the only character, the in-game credit reads "Herói: Ozzbit Games".

## Amendment: a third model, Kratos

A third model, Kratos, is also the owner's own pixel art (no credit, `credit` null in `kratos.json`). It takes slot 6, which was the green-caped skeleton; the skeleton keeps slots 4, 5 and 7 with three capes, so every other slot looks as it did. The source is a single GIF in gitignored `assets-src/kratos/kratos.gif`: eight 64×64 frames of the character turning on the spot, with no game animation at all. The pipeline reads it with a small GIF decoder (`tools/sprites/src/gif.ts`) and the recipe (`tools/sprites/src/kratos.ts`) takes only the right-facing side frame and draws all seven animations from it: the frame is split at the hip into torso and legs, the legs become two (the far one darkened, drawn underneath) that swing from the hip and tuck at the knee, and the torso leans and bobs; the shove steps forward and extends the sword hand. As with the skeleton's drawn frames, this is a stand-in until the owner draws real sheets. The character is 62 pixels tall at 1:1, taller than the hero (37) and the skeleton (51); it isn't scaled down because pixel art doesn't survive it.

## Amendment: a fourth model, Vorcaro, and a ninth slot

A fourth model, Vorcaro (a man in a suit), is art the owner had an image model make from reference pictures (no credit, `credit` null in `vorcaro.json`). Characters stopped being exclusive, so it doesn't take anyone's slot: `CHARACTERS` goes from 8 to 9 and it is slot 8, while a room still holds at most eight people. The source is seven sheets in gitignored `assets-src/vorcaro/`, one per animation, in 256×384 cells. Unlike the other packs this is not pixel art at game size: the character is about 300 pixels tall. A first version shrank it 6× in the recipe with a dominant-colour filter, enlarged one run frame and dropped two duplicate frames; the owner rejected that, because the result was no longer the art. So the rule for this model is that **the recipe changes no pixel**: it only moves frames (every frame's lowest point onto one ground line, and the run 24 pixels forward so the feet sit under the body) and crops them all to one rectangle. The committed sheet is the art at its own size (1920×2135), and the atlas carries `scale: 1/6`, world units per frame pixel. The client multiplies every atlas number by it (`artScale` in `apps/web/src/lib/sprites/characters.ts`): the world sprite, the post-it height, the picker portrait and the face swatch, with smooth filtering for this sheet only. He stands about 50 units tall.

## Amendment: Kratos redrawn, and one recipe for image-model packs

Kratos's turnaround GIF and the recipe that drew his animations in code are gone. The owner had an image model make a full set for him too: seven sheets in `assets-src/kratos/`, 116×160 cells, with a `sheet.json` describing them. He keeps slot 6 and his UI colour.

Since both image-model characters follow the same rules, they share one recipe, `tools/sprites/src/pack.ts`: it changes no pixel, drops every frame's lowest point onto the ground line, optionally shifts an animation sideways, and writes the sheet at the art's size with `scale` in the atlas. `kratos.ts` and `vorcaro.ts` are only numbers (`PackConfig`). Kratos is drawn at 1/2 (about 60 units tall, as before); his sheet is lossless WebP like Vorcaro's. The GIF decoder (`gif.ts`) had no other user and was removed. The prompt the owner gives the image model is kept in `docs/character-prompt.md`, and the import steps in `docs/art.md`.

## Amendment: the cast cut to six, one per model

With four image-model characters in, the owner removed the colour variants: the hero keeps only the blonde hair and the skeleton only the red cape. `CHARACTERS` goes from 11 to 6 and the slots are renumbered in list order: 0 hero, 1 skeleton, 2 Kratos, 3 Vorcaro, 4 Orelha, 5 Bolsonaro. `HAIRS` and `CAPES` stay as lists of one, so a variant can come back as one line plus a slot. Browsers remember the last character by number; a number that now points elsewhere just selects that character, and one out of range falls back to slot 0. Sheets of the removed slots are deleted from `apps/web/public/sprites/`; an override for a file name that no longer exists (ADR 0009) is simply never served.

## Amendment: one size rule, two resizes, and packs that choose their frame counts

Sizes were picked by eye at each import. The owner asked for a rule: Eve and Pinocchio are the normal size, a dog reaches their knees, a big character is taller. So the reference is an ordinary adult, 50 world units (`NORMAL_HEIGHT`), drawn 128 px tall in the art (`NORMAL_ART_HEIGHT`); the character prompt makes the model pick a size as a multiple of that and draw at that many pixels, so new packs all import at one scale (`PACK_WORLD_SCALE`). Two existing characters were resized to the rule with `worldScaleFor`: Orelha from 0.6 to 0.4 of an adult (20 units tall, knee to mid-thigh), and Bolsonaro on the tyrannosaur from 0.9 to 1.4 (70 tall, 80 long, now the largest), so the rider is about person-sized. Their sheets are unchanged; only `scale` in the atlases moved. The others stay as they were (the hero at 0.74 and the knight at 0.69 are meant to be small).

The prompt also stopped fixing frame counts: it gives a minimum per animation and a duration, and the model decides how many frames each needs. `packSpec` builds a pack's spec from the numbers in its `sheet.json`, and `buildPack` rejects timings the game can't play (an attack longer than `SHOVE_COOLDOWN_MS`, a fall that doesn't last `FALL_MS`, which `@guess/world` now exports).

## Amendment: at least 8 frames, 18 for the attack, and an attack that may leave the cell

The owner raised the prompt's minimums: every animation has at least 8 frames and the attack at least 18, and the attack may reach outside the character's cell. The game still shows the attack for `SHOVE_COOLDOWN_MS` (0.45 s), so 18 frames play at 40 fps; the limits in `pack.ts` moved to 24 frames and 60 fps. For the reach, `attack.png` may have a larger cell than the other sheets: `PackConfig.cells` gives an animation its own cell size and the offset that puts its feet where the idle's are. Because every frame of a model is cropped to one rectangle, a far-reaching attack widens all of them; `buildPack` rejects a sheet over 8192 px on a side instead of producing a texture some machines can't load. No existing pack uses either feature yet.

## Amendment: a registry, and seven more characters

Each new character had meant touching about twenty places (two type unions, the tool's model list, the client's imports, CSS variables nothing read, six tests and several documents). Now a seven-sheet character is **one entry in `PACKS`** (`tools/sprites/src/packs.ts`) plus one more in `CHARACTERS`. The tool builds every entry, writes all atlases into one `atlases.json` that the client imports, and the tests iterate the registry. The per-model atlas files and the `--gs-char-N` variables are gone. The picker scrolls, showing two rows and part of a third.

Seven packs came with this change, all from the current prompt, sized by their `sheet.json` and imported with no pixel changed (slots 13 to 19, `CHARACTERS` 20): Star Platinum, Josuke, Joker (Persona), Giorno Giovanna, Zed, and two of the owner himself, Guimas in street clothes and as an acolyte. They are new drawings generated for the owner (the first five in the likeness of characters from JoJo's Bizarre Adventure, Persona 5 and League of Legends), not extracted game art. Two needed something new in `PackConfig`:

- **`float`**. Star Platinum hovers: his walk, run and attack frames sit a few pixels above the ground, each at its own height. Dropping every frame to the ground would have removed the hover and made the frames jitter, so those animations keep the height the art gave them, measured from the idle's ground line.
- **`files`**. Josuke's `fall.png` is a landing (down to the floor and back to idle), drawn that way at the owner's request, but the game plays `fall` at the top of the jump, where a landing makes no sense. His `fall` therefore uses the `fall_loop.png` sheet, and the landing is unused until the game has a landing animation.

The owner also set the masked knight to 0.2 of an adult (10 units tall, from 35): the smallest character, below a person's knee and smaller than the dog.

## Amendment: Jotaro, Miku, Galo Doido and a redrawn Zed; attacks that last their own length; framed previews

Four packs from the prompt that asks for at least 8 frames everywhere, 18 in the attack, and lets the attack use a larger cell. All imported with no pixel changed, at `PACK_WORLD_SCALE` (`CHARACTERS` 23):

- **Zed**, redrawn (slot kept): size 1.10, an attack cell of 256×176 against 192×176, 24 attack frames in 0.65 s.
- **Jotaro with Star Platinum** beside him: size 1.19, an attack cell of 384×224, 24 frames in 0.9 s. The Stand hovers; Jotaro's feet are the lowest point of every frame, so grounding leaves the hover alone. The atlas gained `face`: `head` marks the top of the pair (where the post-it goes), `face` is Jotaro's own face for the UI.
- **Miku** (drawn muscular): size 0.91, a high kick in `shove.png`.
- **Galo Doido**, the rooster mascot: size 1.09, an attack cell of 240×176 in which he stands 40 px further right, so the attack frames move 40 px back (`cells.shove.dx`).

All are new drawings generated for the owner, in the likeness of characters from League of Legends, JoJo's Bizarre Adventure and Vocaloid and of a football club's mascot; none is extracted game art.

**Attacks last their own length.** Two of these attacks run longer than `SHOVE_COOLDOWN_MS` at the owner's request. Rather than cut them or speed them up, the world now locks the attacker for the length of their character's attack (`shoveLock`: at least `SHOVE_COOLDOWN_MS`, at most `SHOVE_MAX_MS` = 1.2 s), passed in as `StepCtx.shoveMs` from the atlas. A slow attack is therefore a real cost: you can't attack again until it ends. The prompt now asks for attacks of 0.7 to 1.2 s, with the duration and pacing worked out from the attack's range of motion and force.

**Previews are framed.** The picker and the home stage showed every character in one shared window at one scale, so with a dog at knee height and a rider on a dinosaur some were cut off and others sat tiny at the bottom. `Hero.svelte` now frames each character by its own standing box, scaled to fill its cell (`fitScale`); the shared `PORTRAIT` window is gone. True relative sizes are in the game and in the `/sistema` line-up.

## Amendment: sheet pages and lazy loading

Two problems with one-sheet-per-character: the Vault Boy's 8760 px sheet failed to upload on GPUs capped at 8192 (software WebGL included), and Pixi's batching turned that into a black rectangle over the middle roof; and every visit decoded all thirty sheets, about 250 MB as RGBA in the page and more in the GPU process, to draw the few characters in the room.

- **`MAX_SHEET` is back to 8192, and a character's sheet is split into pages** (`paginate` in `tools/sprites/src/atlas.ts`): `char-N-idle` (the idle, one line) and `char-N-moves` (the other six animations, each starting on a new line and wrapping at `cols` frames, with `cols` chosen for a near-square page). Only whole frames move; a check over all 1813 frames confirmed every one is byte-identical to the old sheet's. The atlas gains `pages` and a `page` per animation. The tightest packing would also wrap animations into each other, but a page where each animation starts on its own line is easier for the owner to read and edit when replacing a file from `/sistema`.
- **New file names**: an override of the old `char-N.webp` (ADR 0009) can't mask a page, because no page has that name. `/sistema` previews, downloads and replaces each page on its own.
- **Lazy loading**: the roof loads only the characters of the room's members and bots, idle page first; it frees a sheet unused for a minute and, once quiet, downloads the rest into the HTTP cache without decoding. The picker, the stage and the face square only use the idle page. Measured with the audit's script on a desktop GL: the page process went from 377 to 168 MB on the home screen and from 771 to 208 MB with the roof showing; after switching through all thirty characters, 964 to 384 MB, and the GPU process 1040 to 354 MB.
- **A defensive check**: the client reads `MAX_TEXTURE_SIZE` and never uploads a larger texture; a sheet that doesn't fit is shrunk in GPU memory only, and drawn larger by the same factor. Stored art keeps its full resolution (`docs/art.md`: supplied pixels never change).
